[F1, F3, F4, given]

Clause 1, representation and continuity: by the ideal law, $R(t)\cdot\delta=0$ for every $\delta\in\ker D_{x}G(t,x(t))$; the Jacobian is surjective because its rank is $k$ at $(t,x(t))\in\Sigma$ by [F1]. Applying clause 1 of [F2] at each $t$ gives a unique $\lambda(t)\in\mathbb R^{k}$ with $R(t)=D_{x}G(t,x(t))^{\mathsf T}\lambda(t)$. By clause 2 of [F2], $\lambda(t)=C(t,x(t))^{-1}D_{x}G(t,x(t))\mathsf M^{-1}R(t)$; here $t\mapsto C(t,x(t))$ is $C^{1}$ (indeed $C^{2}$) because $G$ is $C^{3}$ and $x$ is $C^{2}$, its values are invertible with $C^{-1}$ continuous by [F6], and $R$ is continuous by the definition of a reaction field; hence $\lambda$ is continuous. [F1, F2, F6, given, algebra]

Clause 1, explicit value: applying [F5] to the constrained motion and using the model equation $\mathsf Mx''=F(t,x,w)+R$ of [F1] together with $R=D_{x}G^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ of step 1.2, $$0=\frac{d^{2}}{dt^{2}}G\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)=G_{tt}+2G_{tq}[w]+G_{qq}[w,w]+D_{x}G\,\mathsf M^{-1}\bigl(F+D_{x}G^{\mathsf T}\lambda\bigr)=G_{tt}+2G_{tq}[w]+G_{qq}[w,w]+D_{x}G\,\mathsf M^{-1}F+C\lambda,$$ where $C=D_{x}G\,\mathsf M^{-1}D_{x}G^{\mathsf T}$ is evaluated at $(t,x(t))$; solving, $C\lambda=-\bigl[D_{x}G\mathsf M^{-1}F+G_{tt}+2G_{tq}[w]+G_{qq}[w,w]\bigr]=C\,\Lambda(t,x,w)$ with $\Lambda$ of [F3], and $C$ is invertible, so $\lambda(t)=\Lambda(t,x(t),w(t))$. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

Clauses 1 and 2, regularity and forward direction: by [F3], $C$ is symmetric positive definite and invertible and $\Lambda,a$ are $C^{1}$ on $O'\times\mathbb R^{3N}$; composing with the $C^{1}$ curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t),w(t))$ shows that $\lambda$ is $C^{1}$ as well, completing clause 1. Moreover $x'=w$ and $w'=x''=\mathsf M^{-1}(F+D_{x}G^{\mathsf T}\lambda)=\mathsf M^{-1}(F+D_{x}G^{\mathsf T}\Lambda(t,x,w))=a(t,x,w)$ by step 2.1, so $(x,w)$ solves the system of clause 2. [F3, step 1.2, step 2.1]

Clause 2, converse: let $(x,v)$ be a solution of the system on an interval $J$ with consistent data, and define $R(t):=D_{x}G(t,x(t))^{\mathsf T}\Lambda(t,x(t),v(t))$; $R$ is continuous because $\Lambda$, $D_{x}G$ and the curve are, and $R(t)\cdot\delta=\Lambda(t,x(t),v(t))\cdot D_{x}G(t,x(t))\delta=0$ for every $\delta\in\ker D_{x}G(t,x(t))$ by [F7], so the ideal-reaction law holds along $(x,v)$. Conversely, every ideal constrained motion with permitted velocity satisfies the system by steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 3.1 applied to it: the hypotheses (h1)-(h2) and the structure of [F4] are the same. The uniqueness and maximal existence of solutions through consistent data is clause 2 of [F3]; this completes clause 2. [F3, F7, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]
Clause 3: for a solution with consistent data, clause 3 of [F3] gives $G(t,x(t))=0$ and $G_{t}(t,x(t))+D_{x}G(t,x(t))v(t)=0$ on the maximal interval; this is clause 3. [F3, step 4.1]

Let $G:O\to\mathbb R^k$ be a $C^2$ regular holonomic constraint with $G_q(t,q)$ of rank $k$ on $O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-cm-holonomic-constraint-and-ideal-reactions]]), and let $M\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric positive definite.

Adopt a holonomic-constraint model of [[def-cm06-holonomic-constraint-model]] with datum $(O,k,G)$, mass operator $\mathsf M$, force map $F$, and the ideal-reaction law of [[post-cm06-ideal-reaction-law]].

Adopt the force model and one inertial frame of
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]], with configuration domain $Q$, time
window $I_{0}$ and force map $F$. Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]]
and gradients are Euclidean ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]); points of
$Q$ are written $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$ with $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$.

**(a) Potential representation of the force map.** A model **presents its
force map through a potential** when it declares a function
$$U:I_{0}\times Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$
of class $C^{2}$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), of
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules), with
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N)$$
for every $(t,x,v)$ of the state domain; here $\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is the
gradient of $u\mapsto U(t,x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},u,x_{i+1},\dots,x_{N})$ at
$u=x_{i}$. More generally, a model may declare **residual forces**
$d_{i}:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of the standing
regularity of clause (iii) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and present
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)+d_{i}(t,x,v);$$
the pair $(U,d)$ is then the model's presentation and
$F_{i}^{\mathrm{p}}:=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is its **potential part**. The scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** for the model's potential part; the framework's
earlier admission of potentials in [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (iii) is
the special case $d\equiv0$. A model that presents its whole force map this
way with $d\equiv0$ is a **global potential model** (the term "conservative
model" is used only in this sense).

**(b) Potential and mechanical energy along a curve family.** For a curve
family $x:J\to Q$ of the model ([[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]]
clause (a)) define the **potential energy along the family** and the
**mechanical energy** by
$$U_{x}(t):=U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad E(t):=K(t)+U_{x}(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
with $K$ the kinetic energy of the definition. The potential part contributes
to the force field but not directly to $K$; $E$ is defined only along the
potential branch of the model, and along a motion it is the subject of the
energy balance of this page.

**(c) Normalization of the potential.** Let $c:I_0\to\mathbb R$ be
differentiable and put $\widetilde U:=U+c(t)$, retaining $C^2$ regularity
when a potential presentation of the standing class is required. The spatial
gradient is unchanged, so this presents the same potential part with the same
residual forces. The full converse is componentwise: if $\widetilde U$ and
$U$ are $C^2$ and have the same spatial gradient, then on each connected
component $C$ of the open set $Q$ there is a $C^2$ function
$c_C:I_0\to\mathbb R$ with
$$\widetilde U(t,x)-U(t,x)=c_C(t)\qquad(x\in C).$$
Here a connected component is a maximal connected subset of $Q$. For fixed
$t$, the difference is constant on every ball contained in $Q$: along any
segment in the ball its derivative is the vanishing spatial gradient paired
with the segment direction. The difference is consequently locally constant,
and on a connected component it is constant, since a value's level set and
its complement are both relatively open. Evaluating at any fixed point of
$C$ gives the $C^2$ regularity of $c_C$. Conversely, independent such functions
on the components give a $C^2$ potential with unchanged spatial gradient;
components of an open Euclidean set are open, because each sufficiently small
ball about one of their points is connected and lies in that component.
A single $c(t)$ describes every ambiguity precisely when the component
functions agree, in particular when $Q$ is connected. No agreement follows
from openness alone: on two disjoint balls the potentials $0$ and the function
equal to $0$ on one ball and $1$ on the other have the same force. Every
continuous motion on an interval remains in one component, so its energy
shifts by that component's $c_C(t)$ and its energy rate by $c_C'(t)$.
The representative is part of the model's declaration, and every energy
statement names it.

**(d) Closed and exact force fields.** A **time- and velocity-independent
force field** is an external single-label contribution of the special form
$F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t,x,v)=\varphi_{i}(x)$, read as the map
$\varphi=(\varphi_{1},\dots,\varphi_{N}):Q\to\mathbb R^{3N}$. Such a field is
**closed** when $\partial_{k}\varphi_{j}=\partial_{j}\varphi_{k}$ at every
point of $Q$ (all partial derivatives continuous), and **exact with potential
energy $U$** when $\varphi=-\nabla U$ for a $C^{2}$ function $U:Q\to\mathbb
R$; equivalently, the field $-\varphi$ is exact in the sense of
[[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]] with potential $U$. The following
mathematical facts are used, with their proofs at the cited items:

1. every exact field is closed, by equality of mixed partial derivatives
   ([[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]]);
2. on a star-shaped open domain every closed $C^{1}$ field is exact, by the
   Poincaré lemma ([[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]]);
3. beyond item 2 this item asserts **no** implication from closedness to
   global exactness: on a general open domain a closed field need not have a
   potential energy, and the criterion used by the framework is exactness as
   defined above.

Consequently the existence of a global potential energy on the model's
configuration domain is a property of the field on that domain, and a model
whose potential part is a merely closed field on a non-star-shaped domain is
not thereby a global potential model. The distinction is sharp: the
companion examples page carries a model on an annular domain whose force
field is smooth and closed, has nonzero circulation around a closed loop, and
therefore admits no global potential and no global conserved energy of the
form $K+U$, while item 2 provides a local potential and a locally conserved
energy on every star-shaped subpart of that domain.

**(e) Local potentials.** Let $V\subseteq Q$ be open and star-shaped with
respect to one of its points ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]) and let
$\varphi$ be closed on $V$. Then item 2 of (d) provides a $C^{2}$ potential
$U_{V}:V\to\mathbb R$ with $\varphi|_{V}=-\nabla U_{V}$: a **local potential**
of the field on $V$. On the restricted configuration domain $V$ the model
with force $-\nabla U_{V}$ is a global potential model, so the mechanical
energy $K+U_{V}$ is available along curve families in $V$; this is how a
potential is recovered from a merely closed field on a sufficiently small
star-shaped piece of the domain, with no claim of a global representative.

**(f) Equipotential level sets.** Let $U:Q\to\mathbb R$ be $C^{2}$, let
$c\in\mathbb R$ and suppose $U^{-1}(c)\neq\varnothing$ and $\nabla
U(x)\neq0$ for every $x\in U^{-1}(c)$; equivalently $c$ is a regular value of
$U$ and every point of the level set is a regular point
([[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]]). Then $U^{-1}(c)$ is an
embedded submanifold of $Q$ of dimension $3N-1$
([[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]],
[[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]). No such conclusion is made at a
level where $\nabla U$ vanishes somewhere on the level set, where the level
set may have singular points.

**(g) Status.** The potential, its normalization, the residual forces and the
declaration of a potential presentation are model data; the closed/exact
statements of (d)-(f) are cited mathematics about the declared field. This
item asserts no conservation law, no force law of nature and no measured
value.

derivations.claim: Clause 1, power identity: by [L1] and [L5], $R(t)\cdot w(t)=(D_{x}G(t,x(t))^{\mathsf T}\lambda(t))\cdot w(t)=\lambda(t)\cdot D_{x}G(t,x(t))w(t)=-\lambda(t)\cdot G_{t}(t,x(t))$, using the differentiated constraint $G_{t}+D_{x}Gw=0$ of [L1]. [L1, L5, algebra]

Clause 1, scleronomic case and integral: if the datum is scleronomic, then by [L6] the point $(t,x(t))$ lies in $\Sigma$ and $G_{t}(t,x(t))=0$ for every $t\in J$, so step 1.1 gives $R(t)\cdot w(t)=0$; both integrals of clause 1 vanish. In general, $t\mapsto R(t)\cdot w(t)$ is continuous (it is a finite sum of products of continuous functions, [L5]) and the displayed integrals are its integrals and those of $-\lambda\cdot G_{t}$, which are equal by step 1.1. [step 1.1, L5, L6]

earlier admission of potentials in [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (iii) is
the special case $d\equiv0$. A model that presents its whole force map this
way with $d\equiv0$ is a **global potential model** (the term "conservative
model" is used only in this sense).

family $x:J\to Q$ of the model ([[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]]
clause (a)) define the **potential energy along the family** and the
**mechanical energy** by
$$U_{x}(t):=U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad E(t):=K(t)+U_{x}(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
with $K$ the kinetic energy of the definition. The potential part contributes
to the force field but not directly to $K$; $E$ is defined only along the
potential branch of the model, and along a motion it is the subject of the
energy balance of this page.

differentiable and put $\widetilde U:=U+c(t)$, retaining $C^2$ regularity
when a potential presentation of the standing class is required. The spatial
gradient is unchanged, so this presents the same potential part with the same
residual forces. The full converse is componentwise: if $\widetilde U$ and
$U$ are $C^2$ and have the same spatial gradient, then on each connected
component $C$ of the open set $Q$ there is a $C^2$ function
$c_C:I_0\to\mathbb R$ with

segment in the ball its derivative is the vanishing spatial gradient paired
with the segment direction. The difference is consequently locally constant,
and on a connected component it is constant, since a value's level set and
its complement are both relatively open. Evaluating at any fixed point of
$C$ gives the $C^2$ regularity of $c_C$. Conversely, independent such functions
on the components give a $C^2$ potential with unchanged spatial gradient;
components of an open Euclidean set are open, because each sufficiently small
ball about one of their points is connected and lies in that component.
A single $c(t)$ describes every ambiguity precisely when the component
functions agree, in particular when $Q$ is connected. No agreement follows
from openness alone: on two disjoint balls the potentials $0$ and the function
equal to $0$ on one ball and $1$ on the other have the same force. Every
continuous motion on an interval remains in one component, so its energy
shifts by that component's $c_C(t)$ and its energy rate by $c_C'(t)$.
The representative is part of the model's declaration, and every energy
statement names it.

   potential energy, and the criterion used by the framework is exactness as

configuration domain is a property of the field on that domain, and a model
whose potential part is a merely closed field on a non-star-shaped domain is
not thereby a global potential model. The distinction is sharp: the
companion examples page carries a model on an annular domain whose force
field is smooth and closed, has nonzero circulation around a closed loop, and
therefore admits no global potential and no global conserved energy of the
form $K+U$, while item 2 provides a local potential and a locally conserved

$F_{i}^{\mathrm{p}}:=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is its **potential part**. The scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** for the model's potential part; the framework's
earlier admission of potentials in [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (iii) is
the special case $d\equiv0$. A model that presents its whole force map this
way with $d\equiv0$ is a **global potential model** (the term "conservative
model" is used only in this sense).

**(b) Potential and mechanical energy along a curve family.** For a curve
family $x:J\to Q$ of the model ([[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]]
clause (a)) define the **potential energy along the family** and the
**mechanical energy** by
$$U_{x}(t):=U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad E(t):=K(t)+U_{x}(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
with $K$ the kinetic energy of the definition. The potential part contributes
to the force field but not directly to $K$; $E$ is defined only along the
potential branch of the model, and along a motion it is the subject of the
energy balance of this page.

**(c) Normalization of the potential.** Let $c:I_0\to\mathbb R$ be
differentiable and put $\widetilde U:=U+c(t)$, retaining $C^2$ regularity
when a potential presentation of the standing class is required. The spatial
gradient is unchanged, so this presents the same potential part with the same
residual forces. The full converse is componentwise: if $\widetilde U$ and
$U$ are $C^2$ and have the same spatial gradient, then on each connected
component $C$ of the open set $Q$ there is a $C^2$ function
$c_C:I_0\to\mathbb R$ with
$$\widetilde U(t,x)-U(t,x)=c_C(t)\qquad(x\in C).$$
Here a connected component is a maximal connected subset of $Q$. For fixed
$t$, the difference is constant on every ball contained in $Q$: along any
segment in the ball its derivative is the vanishing spatial gradient paired
with the segment direction. The difference is consequently locally constant,
and on a connected component it is constant, since a value's level set and
its complement are both relatively open. Evaluating at any fixed point of
$C$ gives the $C^2$ regularity of $c_C$. Conversely, independent such functions
on the components give a $C^2$ potential with unchanged spatial gradient;
components of an open Euclidean set are open, because each sufficiently small
ball about one of their points is connected and lies in that component.
A single $c(t)$ describes every ambiguity precisely when the component
functions agree, in particular when $Q$ is connected. No agreement follows
from openness alone: on two disjoint balls the potentials $0$ and the function
equal to $0$ on one ball and $1$ on the other have the same force. Every
continuous motion on an interval remains in one component, so its energy
shifts by that component's $c_C(t)$ and its energy rate by $c_C'(t)$.
The representative is part of the model's declaration, and every energy
statement names it.

**(d) Closed and exact force fields.** A **time- and velocity-independent
force field** is an external single-label contribution of the special form
$F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t,x,v)=\varphi_{i}(x)$, read as the map
$\varphi=(\varphi_{1},\dots,\varphi_{N}):Q\to\mathbb R^{3N}$. Such a field is
**closed** when $\partial_{k}\varphi_{j}=\partial_{j}\varphi_{k}$ at every
point of $Q$ (all partial derivatives continuous), and **exact with potential
energy $U$** when $\varphi=-\nabla U$ for a $C^{2}$ function $U:Q\to\mathbb
R$; equivalently, the field $-\varphi$ is exact in the sense of
[[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]] with potential $U$. The following
mathematical facts are used, with their proofs at the cited items:

1. every exact field is closed, by equality of mixed partial derivatives
   ([[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]]);
2. on a star-shaped open domain every closed $C^{1}$ field is exact, by the
   Poincaré lemma ([[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]]);
3. beyond item 2 this item asserts **no** implication from closedness to
   global exactness: on a general open domain a closed field need not have a
   potential energy, and the criterion used by the framework is exactness as
   defined above.

Consequently the existence of a global potential energy on the model's
configuration domain is a property of the field on that domain, and a model
whose potential part is a merely closed field on a non-star-shaped domain is
not thereby a global potential model. The distinction is sharp: the
companion examples page carries a model on an annular domain whose force
field is smooth and closed, has nonzero circulation around a closed loop, and
therefore admits no global potential and no global conserved energy of the
form $K+U$, while item 2 provides a local potential and a locally conserved
energy on every star-shaped subpart of that domain.

**(e) Local potentials.** Let $V\subseteq Q$ be open and star-shaped with
respect to one of its points ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]) and let
$\varphi$ be closed on $V$. Then item 2 of (d) provides a $C^{2}$ potential
$U_{V}:V\to\mathbb R$ with $\varphi|_{V}=-\nabla U_{V}$: a **local potential**
of the field on $V$. On the restricted configuration domain $V$ the model
with force $-\nabla U_{V}$ is a global potential model, so the mechanical
energy $K+U_{V}$ is available along curve families in $V$; this is how a
potential is recovered from a merely closed field on a sufficiently small
star-shaped piece of the domain, with no claim of a global representative.

$U$ and every point of the level set is a regular point
([[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]]). Then $U^{-1}(c)$ is an
embedded submanifold of $Q$ of dimension $3N-1$
([[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]],
[[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]). No such conclusion is made at a
level where $\nabla U$ vanishes somewhere on the level set, where the level
set may have singular points.

derivations.claim: The M1 constraint data and its holonomic-equivalence: $\mathcal G_{q}=(1,-a)$ has rank one, $\ker\mathcal G_{q}=\{(a\delta,\delta):\delta\in\mathbb R\}$ as a set of virtual displacements, and along any admissible curve $x'-a\theta'=0$; hence $\mathcal G(q(t))$ is constant by [F4], so the constraint is the differentiated position constraint $\mathcal G=$ constant and is holonomic-equivalent in the sense of [F5]. [F2, F4, F5, algebra]

The M1 acceleration, multiplier and reaction: by [F1] with the time-independent data of [F2], $C=\mathcal G_{q}M^{-1}\mathcal G_{q}^{\mathsf T}=\frac1m+\frac{a^{2}}{I}=\frac{I+ma^{2}}{mI}$, $\mathcal G_{q}M^{-1}\Phi=\frac{f}{m}$, and $\Lambda=-C^{-1}\frac fm=-\frac{mI}{I+ma^{2}}\cdot\frac fm=-\frac{fI}{I+ma^{2}}=\lambda$. The equations $Mq''=\Phi+\mathcal G_{q}^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ read $mx''=f+\lambda$ and $I\theta''=-a\lambda$; substituting $\lambda$ gives $mx''=f-\frac{fI}{I+ma^{2}}=\frac{fma^{2}}{I+ma^{2}}$, that is $x''=\frac{fa^{2}}{I+ma^{2}}$, and $I\theta''=\frac{afI}{I+ma^{2}}$, that is $\theta''=\frac{af}{I+ma^{2}}$; this is the displayed triple, with reaction $\mathcal G_{q}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=(\lambda,-a\lambda)$. The reaction power vanishes because $R\cdot q'=\lambda x'-a\lambda\theta'=\lambda(x'-a\theta')=0$ by the constraint, in agreement with the power identity of [F1] and $\mathcal G_{t}=0$. [F1, F2, algebra]
The M2 acceleration: by [F3], $x''=f/m$ and $\theta''=0$. [F3, algebra]

The models disagree and the comparison is quantitative: for $f\ne0$, subtracting the two predictions gives $x''_{\mathrm{M2}}-x''_{\mathrm{M1}}=\frac fm-\frac{fa^{2}}{I+ma^{2}}=\frac{f}{m}\cdot\frac{I}{I+ma^{2}}\ne0$, so the two declared models are distinct; taking the ratio, $\frac{x''_{\mathrm{M1}}}{x''_{\mathrm{M2}}}=\frac{ma^{2}}{I+ma^{2}}=\frac{1}{1+I/(ma^{2})}$, which is $\frac{2}{3}$ at $I=\frac12ma^{2}$ and $\frac12$ at $I=ma^{2}$. [F3, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

The contact capability condition: model M1's reaction is the contact's force pair $(\lambda,-a\lambda)$ with $|\lambda|=\frac{|f|I}{I+ma^{2}}$; a contact model with normal reaction $N$ and static-friction bound $\mu_{s}$ can maintain no-slip only while the required tangential force satisfies $|\lambda|\le\mu_{s}N$. For the uniform disk $I=\frac12ma^{2}$ this is $\frac{|f|}{3}\le\mu_{s}N$, that is $|f|\le3\mu_{s}N$; with the weight-only normal reaction $N=mg$ on a horizontal plane, $|f|\le3\mu_{s}mg$. Where the bound fails, the no-slip idealization is not a valid model of that contact; the sliding model or a kinetic-friction model applies instead, and transitions between rolling and slipping — like general three-dimensional rolling and rank or contact changes — are outside the present comparison. [F5, step 1.2, algebra]

Finite model data: with $m=1$, $a=1$, $I=\frac12$, $f=3$ and $g=10$ one has $x''_{\mathrm{M1}}=\frac{3\cdot1}{\frac12+1}=2\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-2}$, $x''_{\mathrm{M2}}=3\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $\lambda=-\frac{3\cdot\frac12}{\frac12+1}=-1\,\mathrm N$, so the required tangential force is $1\,\mathrm N$; with the declared $\mu_{s}=\frac12$ and $N=mg=10\,\mathrm N$ the bound $\mu_{s}N=5\,\mathrm N$ is satisfied and M1 is consistent with the declared contact model on these data. With $f=18$ instead, $x''_{\mathrm{M1}}=12\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $\lambda=-6\,\mathrm N$, whose magnitude exceeds $5\,\mathrm N$, so the required force lies outside the declared contact capability and M1's premises fail. [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.2, algebra]

Clauses 1-5 are proved: the reduced ideal no-slip model and the frictionless sliding model have the displayed accelerations, they are distinct for every nonzero applied force, the ideal model's reaction is the displayed contact pair with vanishing power, and the contact capability condition selects the models on explicit data. The example is a comparison of declared reduced models, not a derivation of the disk's reduction from rigid-body mechanics and not a measurement.
